Article Title: Meloni plans burqa, niqab ban in Italian schools; how it compares to rest of Europe
Article Text:
Italy moves to ban burqa, niqab in schools, says Meloni (AI-generated image)

What exactly is Italy proposing?

How does Italy compare with the rest of Europe?

Italy is preparing to ban the burqa and niqab in schools, Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni announced on Sunday, putting the country back in the spotlight of Europe’s long-running debate over face-covering veils, religious expression and integration.Meloni said her government would soon take a measure to the Cabinet that would prohibit burqas and niqabs in schools. She also proposed limiting the number of foreign students in each classroom and requiring parents of foreign students facing serious integration difficulties to learn Italian. The government has not yet specified the proposed limit on foreign students.“You must go to school with your face uncovered,” Meloni said, arguing that no one in Italy should be able to decide that a young woman must hide her face in the name of tradition. The proposed measure still needs to go through the legislative process before it becomes law.The proposal specifically refers to burqas and niqabs, but not hijabs. A burqa covers the entire body and includes a mesh covering over the eyes, while a niqab covers the face but leaves the eyes visible. A hijab covers the hair and neck but leaves the face uncovered.Italy already has a 1975 law restricting the wearing of clothing that makes identification difficult in public places.The issue of full-face veils has previously been dealt with under that framework in certain circumstances, but Italy has not had a nationwide law specifically banning burqas or niqabs in schools.The proposed school ban comes as Italy joins a wider European debate over how far governments can regulate face-covering clothing.There is no single European rule on burqas and niqabs. Countries have taken different approaches, from blanket public-space bans to restrictions in schools, hospitals and public transport, while some have no nationwide face-covering ban at all.It was the first European country to introduce a nationwide ban on clothing that conceals the face in public spaces in 2011. Violations can lead to a fine and, in some cases, a civic education course.It was introduced as a nationwide ban in 2011. Violations can result in fines and prison sentences of up to seven days.Full-face veils have been banned in public spaces since 2016, with wearing them restricted to private homes and places of worship.A nationwide ban on full-face coverings took effect in 2017. Austria has also gone further in schools: from September 2026, girls up to the age of 14 are prohibited from wearing Islamic headscarves that cover the head at school.It introduced a nationwide ban on face-covering clothing in public places in 2018, covering garments including the burqa and niqab.Its 2019 law is narrower, restricting face coverings in places including schools, hospitals, government buildings and public transport rather than imposing a blanket public-space ban.A federal ban on face coverings in public spaces came into force in 2023 after voters approved the measure in a national referendum.It completed legislation in August 2026 banning face coverings in public spaces, with exemptions including health, professional, artistic and religious settings.There is no nationwide blanket ban. Federal rules restrict face coverings in certain circumstances, including for some public employees, judges, members of the armed forces and motorists, while several states have additional restrictions.There is no national ban on religious attire, although some municipalities have attempted school-level restrictions.It has no nationwide ban comparable to France's, with restrictions instead varying according to local or institutional rules.The European debate has therefore moved in different directions. France, Belgium and Denmark prohibit face coverings broadly in public, while countries such as the Netherlands limit them to specific settings.Italy's proposed measure is more narrowly focused on, putting it closer to Austria's approach than to Europe's blanket public-space bans. Whether it becomes law will depend on the legislative process that follows Meloni's Cabinet proposal.
Article Summary: Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said her government would soon take a measure to the Cabinet that would prohibit burqas and niqabs in schools. A burqa covers the entire body and includes a mesh covering over the eyes, while a niqab covers the face but leaves the eyes visible.

Article Title: An Ontario couple paid C$200 for a landscape painting at a rural yard sale; six years later the work was identified as E J Hughes’s Lake Okanagan and sold at auction for C$402,500
Article Text:
Hughes spent much of his career focusing on the landscapes of British Columbia

Hughes’ as a war artist

Hughes' wartime work included detailed drawings and paintings of military life

A quiet life on Vancouver Island

From C$200 yard sale find to millions

An Ontario couple who paid just C$200 for a landscape painting at a rural yard sale in 2001 later discovered that they had bought a work by renowned Canadian artist E J Hughes, literary weboste BC Booklook reported. Six years after the purchase, the painting, Lake Okanagan, was identified as a Hughes work and sold at auction for C$402,500.Hughes, a British Columbia painter's detailed landscapes have gained major value over the years. His work, once bought for a few hundred Canadian dollars, sells for hundreds of thousands and even millions at auction.Hughes is also the focus of a new documentary by Coquitlam filmmaker Jenn Strom. The Painted Life of E J Hughes looks at the artist’s life, his connection with British Columbia and the quiet way in which he worked. The documentary screened at the VIFF Centre in Vancouver in February.Strom became interested in Hughes while researching British Columbia’s history about seven years ago. Her research led her to the work of author Robert Amos, who wrote about Hughes and his life on Vancouver Island.Strom said she was drawn to the artist because his personality was very different from the public image often associated with artists.“He was humble and painfully shy. He didn’t have it in him to be out there promoting his own work,” Strom told Freshet News.Edward John Hughes was born in North Vancouver on February 17, 1913, and grew up in Nanaimo and North Vancouver. During the Depression, he worked on fishing boats before studying at the Vancouver School of Decorative and Applied Art.One of his teachers was Frederick Varley, a member of Canada’s famous Group of Seven artists. Hughes also later co-founded a commercial art company with muralists Paul Goranson and Orville Fisher in 1934.When the Second World War began, Hughes enlisted with the Royal Canadian Artillery in 1939 and was posted to England. From 1943 to 1946, he worked as one of Canada’s official war artists.His wartime work included detailed drawings and paintings of military life. According to literary webiste BC BookLook, Hughes produced about 1,000 drawings and almost 30 complete paintings during his time as a war artist. Around 1,600 of his works are now held by the Canadian War Museum.His role required him to carefully record military equipment, uniforms, people and their surroundings. The detailed observation involved in that work later became an important part of his approach to painting landscapes.After returning to the West Coast in 1946, Hughes settled at Shawnigan Lake with his wife, Fern. Strom filmed the area and the home where the artist lived while making her documentary. “He needed silence. Peace and quiet,” Strom said.Hughes spent much of his career focusing on the landscapes of British Columbia. He was deeply interested in nature and in recording places with careful detail.“I feel that, when I am doing my painting, it is a form of worship,” Hughes said in a 1961 CBC television production.Hughes had also considered whether to focus more on figures or landscapes, but eventually chose landscapes because he felt they represented the British Columbia and Canadian environment strongly and would sell more readily.Despite his growing reputation, he struggled financially at one stage and nearly gave up painting. His career received important support from art dealer Max Stern, who had previously represented Emily Carr.Stern tracked Hughes down at Shawnigan Lake in 1951 after receiving advice from Lawren Harris, a founding member of Canada’s Group of Seven. He later recalled meeting a shy artist who was not fully aware of the quality of his own work. Stern decided to represent him.After their first meeting, Stern bought all the work then available in Hughes’ studio for $500. The relationship helped Hughes build a stronger career while also giving him support in dealing with the public and the art market.The value of Hughes’ work increased significantly as his reputation grew. His painting Lake Okanagan is one of the most striking examples. Bought at an Ontario yard sale for C$200 in 2001, it was sold for C$402,500, six years later.The price was part of a wider rise in the value of Hughes’ paintings. BC BookLook noted that Rivers Inlet sold for $920,000 in 2005, then the highest price paid for a work by a living Canadian artist.Other works have reached even higher prices. Hughes’ Fishboats, River Inlet sold for $2 million at Heffel Auction. In November 2025, his 1949 painting Entrance to Howe Sound sold for $4.8 million.Strom said Hughes’ story continues to attract attention because of the strength of his work and the contrast between his quiet personality and the growing value of his paintings. “His story keeps growing,” she said.
Article Summary: E J Hughes spent much of his career focusing on the landscapes of British Columbia. His work, once bought for a few hundred Canadian dollars, sells for hundreds of thousands and even millions at auction. A new documentary looks at the artist’s life, his connection with British Columbia and the quiet way in which he worked.

Article Title: Australian couple spent $500,000 building their retirement home; it was constructed on the wrong block and later had to be moved 100 metres
Article Text:
Couple had built their home on the neighbour’s block, PC: A Current Affair

The confusion began when the land was still an undivided paddock

Council inspections did not catch the mistake

A proposed land swap failed over differences between the blocks

The house was moved 100 metres onto the correct block

Melanie and David Moor spent more than $500,000 on what they expected to be their retirement home in Camperdown, south-west Victoria, only to discover that the house had been placed entirely on a neighbouring block. The couple had bought land in a new subdivision in 2021 and, after obtaining permits, installed a driveway and relocated a four-bedroom house onto the 2-hectare property they believed they owned. Instead, the house had been moved onto the adjacent block, which belonged to someone else. The mistake was discovered in August 2024, while the Moors were completing work on the house, after a council officer told David Moor to stop construction and seek legal advice. The couple then spent almost two years trying to resolve the dispute, including an unsuccessful proposal to swap the two properties. In April 2026, the house was finally moved about 100 metres onto the block the Moors actually owned.The Moors first viewed the subdivision in August 2021, when the land was still part of a larger 8-hectare paddock that had not yet been divided into individual lots. They paid a $5,000 deposit and signed the contract of sale in April 2022.Melanie Moor told ABC that the couple believed they had identified the correct block after a real estate agent showed them the property, while numbers on nearby fence posts also contributed to their understanding of which lot they had purchased.The real estate agency later said an internal investigation found that its agent had not made false or misleading claims. A spokesperson said the agent had shown the couple the property well before the contract was signed and while it was still part of the larger paddock, adding that it was ultimately the buyers' responsibility to confirm which block they owned. The confusion continued after the purchase. In 2023, before settlement, the Moors had a driveway constructed on the block they believed was theirs, with permission from the former owner of the neighbouring property. When the house was later relocated, the builder and other tradespeople used that driveway as a reference point for identifying the lot. ABC reported that the relocation company's job document listed the road name but not a specific lot number.The Moors obtained a building permit from Corangamite Shire Council in April 2024. However, documents supporting the permit included an aerial photograph showing that soil samples had been taken from the wrong block. Council records also showed that staff visited the site three times in one month to inspect stump holes dug for the house relocation.The mistake was finally identified in August 2024, while the Moors were putting the finishing touches on the house. A council officer contacted David Moor, instructed him to stop work and advised him to seek legal advice. Melanie said the couple initially thought the call was a scam before realising that their new home was sitting entirely on land they did not own. The actual owner of that block lived interstate and had purchased the property from their late uncle. According to the owner's lawyers, the owner had been unaware that the Moors had moved a house onto the land until after the work had taken place.Once the mistake was discovered, the Moors proposed swapping the block where their house had been placed with the neighbouring block they actually owned. The proposal was rejected by the other landowner's lawyers, who said the properties were not equivalent. They pointed to differences in the views from each block, a registered easement on the Moors' property and possible tax consequences from a land swap.The dispute eventually became a legal matter. In July 2025, the landowner's lawyers gave the Moors 14 days to remove the house and restore the property to its original condition, warning that the house could otherwise be sold. At the time, the Moors said they could not afford to move it. The contractor who had originally relocated the house also advised that it might not survive another move. The situation was particularly difficult because Victoria's property laws do not give courts the same range of options available in some other Australian jurisdictions for cases in which someone mistakenly builds on another person's land. An ABC report examining the issue noted that such cases are sometimes referred to as the "mistaken improver" problem.After months of negotiations, the parties reached an agreement in February 2026 for the Moors to clear the disputed property by May 2. The couple eventually found another house mover who was willing to take on the job after their original contractor had warned against a second relocation. Just before Easter, the four-bedroom house was lifted and transported about 100 metres sideways onto the Moors' actual property. The couple described seeing the house transferred onto their own land as a major relief after the prolonged dispute.The move has not yet made the house habitable. The building is temporarily sitting on empty oil drums while it waits to be restumped. Its septic system and electrical wiring had to be disconnected and removed during the relocation, and the Moors said they do not yet know how much structural damage the house may have suffered. Melanie said the house appeared unstable during the move and that the family was not yet comfortable entering it.The couple also have to restore the neighbouring property. They said they need to remove about 160 stumps left where the house had stood and take out trees they had planted before returning the block to its original condition. They estimate the relocation, restumping and reconnection of electricity and other services will cost about $100,000, on top of the more than $500,000 already spent on the home. For now, the Moors have bought a 20-foot caravan and plan to live there with their 20-year-old daughter while they work to make the house liveable. Melanie said the ordeal had taken a significant toll on the family's mental health, but the couple remained determined to finish their retirement home.
Article Summary: Melanie and David Moor spent more than $500,000 on what they expected to be their retirement home in Camperdown, south-west Victoria. The couple bought land in a new subdivision in 2021 and, after obtaining permits, relocated a four- bedroom house onto the 2-hectare property they believed they owned. Instead, the house had been moved onto the adjacent block, which belonged to someone else. Council inspections did not catch the mistake. A proposed land swap failed over differences between the blocks.

Article Title: A couple found a rare Mickey Mantle photo inside a baseball book at a garage sale; it later sold for $20,740
Article Text:
Mickey Mantle, PC: Wikipedia

The photograph captured Mantle as an untested rookie

The image became the basis for Mantle's rookie card

The photograph's reverse carried a matching inscription

A different Type 1 Mantle photograph sold for $843,750

A couple browsing an oversized Topps baseball-card coffee-table book at a local garage sale made an unexpected discovery when they found a rare photograph of a young Mickey Mantle tucked inside. The photograph, later authenticated by PSA/DNA as a Type 2 print, captured Mantle during spring training early in his rookie season and became the source image for his iconic 1951 Bowman rookie card. The couple also found an image of Joe DiMaggio inside the same book, according to Heritage Auctions, which later offered the Mantle photograph for sale. The photograph was sold on December 20, 2025, during Heritage's Winter Sports Catalogue Auction, fetching $20,740. Its value was not simply tied to Mantle's fame. Details in the photograph, including his No. 6 uniform and the bat belonging to teammate Joe Collins, help place the image at a specific point in the young player's career.Heritage's description places the photograph at Arizona spring training, when Mantle was still an untested rookie. One clue is his rolled-up sleeve. The auction house notes that Mantle would later have enough standing to dictate tailoring changes to his uniform, but was not yet in that position at the time the photograph was taken.Another detail is the bat resting over Mantle's right shoulder. Heritage identifies it as a bat belonging to Yankees first baseman Joe Collins. The auction description says Mantle had not yet signed a deal with Hillerich & Bradsby for his own bat, explaining why he was pictured with Collins' equipment instead. The back of Mantle's uniform provides another clue. The visible number is a 6 rather than the No. 7 that became permanently associated with him. Heritage notes that Mantle wore No. 6 only during the unsettled beginning of his rookie campaign before switching to No. 7.The photograph is particularly significant because it became the source for Mantle's 1951 Bowman rookie card. Heritage describes the image as one of the most recognisable photographs of Mantle, although the baseball card altered some of its visual details. The 1951 Bowman version has a distinctive posterised appearance, while Mantle's 1953 Topps card used the same photograph but cropped more tightly around his youthful face. The same image was also used for Mantle's 1952 Berk Ross card. Heritage's records for a separate Type 1 example from the Jack Kramer Collection identify the photograph as the source for the 1951 Bowman and 1953 Topps cards and show Mantle wearing No. 6 with Collins' bat over his shoulder. The garage-sale photograph was classified as Type 2 by PSA/DNA. That distinction matters because it was not one of the rare first-generation prints. Heritage's 2024 records describe the much rarer Type 1 version as an original photograph made from the original negative during the period close to when the picture was taken. PSA's Type 1 classification is based on that first-generation status.The photograph found in the garage-sale book had handwritten words identifying the subject as "Mickey Mantle" on its reverse. Heritage said the handwriting perfectly matched the handwriting on a Type 1 example of the same photograph that it had sold for $71,700 in 2015. The auction house also noted that it had since sold another Type 1 example for more than $800,000.The $20,740 photograph was not in perfect condition. Heritage noted surface wear on the front, numerous light horizontal cracks in the glossy finish, several small areas of paper loss along the white border and a slight tear on the middle-right side. It had no other markings or stamps and was encapsulated by PSA/DNA as a Type 2 photograph. Despite those imperfections, the photograph retained a direct connection to one of the most recognisable images from Mantle's early career. The combination of its provenance, its use as the source for the 1951 Bowman rookie card and its unusual garage-sale discovery helped make it a notable auction find.The huge difference in value between different generations of the image can be seen in another Heritage sale. On April 7, 2024, the auction house sold a Type 1 print of the same Mantle action photograph for $843,750. The photograph came from the collection of Jack Kramer, a former major-league pitcher who had been Mantle's Yankees teammate. It was an original 8-by-10-inch photograph taken by Yankees team photographer Bob Olen and had remained among Kramer's possessions for decades. Heritage said only four known original prints of the image existed, meaning the $843,750 photograph was one of the rare Type 1 examples. The auction house described the sale as a record for a Type 1 sports photograph, surpassing the previous $516,000 record set by a Ty Cobb photograph.The same 2024 auction also included a different Mantle photograph from the Kramer Collection, a 1951 rookie headshot, which sold for $20,625. That was a separate item from the garage-sale photograph that later sold for $20,740. The distinction explains why the two prices, although strikingly similar, should not be confused. The $20,740 sale concerned the Type 2 photograph discovered inside the garage-sale book, while the $20,625 result concerned a separate Kramer Collection headshot. What began as a couple looking through an old baseball book at a local garage sale ultimately uncovered a photograph tied directly to one of Mickey Mantle's most famous baseball-card images. Heritage sold that Type 2 photograph for $20,740 in December 2025.
Article Summary: The photograph captured Mantle during spring training early in his rookie season. It became the source image for his iconic 1951 Bowman rookie card. The couple also found an image of Joe DiMaggio inside the same book. The photograph was sold on December 20, 2025, during Heritage's Winter Sports Catalogue Auction, fetching $20,740.

Article Title: Cats may have their own chemical ‘ID cards’: Scientists found 13 unusual fatty acids in urine that remain stable for at least 24 hours which can easily help identify individual cats
Article Text:
Cats remember individual urine scents

What helps cats distinguish between individual urine

Cats can detect the chemical differences

It seems there exists an established yet hidden cat calling system. According to scientists, cats identify one another through a shockingly durable chemical "calling card" made from 13 unusual fatty acids in their urine. Thus, feline friendships might have to do more with their identification than consistent meetings.Cats rely heavily on scent to learn about one another and often, they gather this information from urine and other odour marks left behind in their surroundings. These chemical traces can continue communicating long after the animal that produced them has moved on.But this leaves us with a puzzle. Many odour molecules evaporate, break down or change over time. If a scent is consistently evolving, how is an animal still able to determine who originally left it? Researchers from Japan, Germany and Spain, led by Iwate University, may have found part of the answer in domestic cats.Their experiments pointed to a group of unusual fatty acids that could serve as a lasting chemical signature in cat urine. The scientists identified 13 branched-chain fatty acids (BFAs). The particular mixture and proportions of these compounds varied from one cat to another, yet remained relatively consistent within the same animal.Behavioural tests also showed that cats could detect differences between BFA profiles when the researchers controlled for other lipids in the urine.The findings suggest that BFAs could function as a durable chemical "calling card" that helps preserve information about individual identity.Before searching for the chemicals involved, the researchers first needed to establish that cats could distinguish between urine from different individuals. When cats encountered the same urine sample repeatedly, they gradually spent less time investigating it. But when urine from a different cat was introduced, their interest rose again, and they spent more time sniffing.Even after gaps lasting months, cats continued to show reduced responses to previously encountered urine odours. This pattern suggested that cats may retain long-term memories of particular urine scents. Researchers also examined the flehmen response, the characteristic open-mouthed expression often seen when cats investigate certain odours. Cats displayed this response more often when smelling unfamiliar urine than when smelling their own.As the same urine was presented repeatedly, the Flehmen response decreased. But when urine from another cat was introduced, the response piqued again. "After confirming that cats can distinguish individual urine odours, we used the flehmen response as a clue to identify urinary molecules that may contribute to individual scent recognition," said Professor Masao Miyazaki of Iwate University, who led the research project.Using the cats' behaviour as a guide, the scientists narrowed their search to a lipid fraction in urine containing unusual BFAs. Ultimately, they identified 13 of these compounds. Interestingly, each cat has a BFA profile defined by the combination and relative abundance of the different fatty acids. Those profiles varied considerably between animals, while remaining comparatively stable when the same cats were sampled on different dates.Genetics also appeared to play some role. Related cats generally had more similar BFA patterns, although each animal still maintained its own distinguishable profile even within the same family. The compounds also proved relatively durable. Many volatile chemicals responsible for urine odour begin changing quickly once urine is deposited. BFAs, by contrast, are semi-volatile and evaporate more slowly.In urine-soaked samples stored at 25°C, the distinctive BFA profiles associated with individual cats remained comparatively stable for at least 24 hours.The researchers then tested whether the cats themselves could actually distinguish these BFA patterns. They controlled other lipid components in the urine samples and changed only the donor-derived BFA-containing fraction. Cats that had already become accustomed to the original sample began sniffing more again when the BFA fraction was switched.That behavioural change provided evidence that cats can perceive differences among individual BFA compositions. The result strengthens the idea that these fatty acids may carry meaningful information about identity rather than simply being unusual chemical byproducts.Moreover, the experiment also produced an unexpected clue involving the kidneys. Researchers detected BFAs in the kidney but not in the other tissues they examined. Lipids containing BFAs were also present among neutral lipids stored inside droplets in the renal cortex.These kidney lipid droplets have puzzled scientists for more than a century, since cats are known to have a large quantity of them, yet their biological purpose remained unidentified. The new findings raise the possibility that the droplets act as a storage reservoir for lipids containing BFAs.Such a reservoir could help keep a cat's chemical signature relatively steady even when diet or physiological conditions temporarily change. By buffering those short-term fluctuations, the kidney might help maintain a more consistent individual chemical profile in urine. "Our findings suggest that one of their functions may be to support a stable chemical signature in urine. How BFAs stored in renal lipids are ultimately released into urine is an important question for future research," said Miyazaki.Moreover, BFA-related compounds in urine and renal lipid droplets were detected in numerous feline species, including lions, tigers, leopards, jaguars, lynxes and the Iriomote cat. The study will be published in Current Biology.
Article Summary: Cats rely heavily on scent to learn about one another and often, they gather this information from urine and other odour marks left behind in their surroundings. Many odour molecules evaporate, break down or change over time. If a scent is consistently evolving, how is an animal still able to determine who originally left it? Researchers from Japan, Germany and Spain, led by Iwate University, may have found part of the answer in domestic cats. Their experiments pointed to a group of unusual fatty acids that could serve as a lasting chemical signature in cat urine.

Article Title: A Florida music hall that hosted Louis Armstrong and Ray Charles closed in 1968; after a four-year, $4.8 million renovation, St Petersburg has reopened it
Article Text:
A new mural by artist Egypt Hagan has been added to the property.

The venue’s Black legacy

Louis Armstrong and his band performed there three times at the venue.

Renovation brings new life

A new community space

St Petersburg’s historic Manhattan Casino reopened on Saturday, 58 years after it closed, following a four-year renovation of the 101-year-old building. According to St Pete Catalyst, the city has spent $4.8 million on the two-storey property, which will now operate as a rentable event space in the Deuces neighbourhood.Built in 1925 by Black businessman Elder Jordan, the venue was originally known as the Jordan Dance Hall and served as a major entertainment centre for the city’s African American community. It hosted live dance music on weekends and gospel performances on Sundays. The building also became a venue for proms, graduations, pageants, parties and conferences.Its upstairs music hall later became known for performances by some of the biggest names in American music. Louis Armstrong and his band performed there three times. Other musicians who appeared at the venue included the Count Basie Orchestra, Ella Fitzgerald, Ray Charles , B B King, Little Richard, Etta James, Sam Cooke, Muddy Waters, Bo Diddley and Otis Redding.The Manhattan Casino was part of The Deuces, a business district that became an important centre for St Petersburg’s African American community during segregation. The venue was also part of the Chitlin’ Circuit, a network of Black-owned venues across the southern United States where Black musicians could perform.The building became especially active during the 1940s and 1950s. Along with visiting performers, it had its own house band, while jazz and swing groups from other parts of the country regularly played for community dances.The history of the building was reflected upon during the reopening. St Petersburg Poet Laureate Denzel Johnson-Green recited his poem, “The Get Down, the Boogie, and the Hope of Sweat”, describing the sounds that once came from the venue.The venue eventually closed in 1968. Several efforts were later made to remodel and revitalise the property, but those attempts did not result in its reopening.The latest project has transformed the historic building into a city-owned event space. The two-storey structure covers 12,000 square feet and is located at 642 22nd Street S.The renovation included changes to both floors. A new first-floor event space was added, along with a conference room, green room, bar and kitchen.The second-floor music hall and ballroom, where many of the famous performers once appeared, also received upgrades. The floors were refinished, the ceiling was raised and new drapery was installed.The restored Jordan Ballroom now forms part of the event space. It is the same upstairs room associated with performances by Armstrong, Fitzgerald, Charles and King, among others.A new mural by artist Egypt Hagan has also been added to the property, giving the renovated building a new visual feature while retaining its connection with its past.St Petersburg Mayor Ken Welch said the renovated building is intended to serve different groups in the community.“This is a totally different model. It’s a community event space that can serve so many constituencies. I think that’s the right model at the right time," Welch said at the event.Welch also said the reopened Manhattan Casino would serve as an anchor for the development of The Deuces and the nearby Warehouse Arts District.For Welch, the reopening also marked the return of a building that has remained part of the city’s history despite being closed for decades.“History does matter, St. Pete,” Welch said during the ceremony. “And so, after four years of renovations, we get to open these doors once again, and begin a new chapter for the Manhattan Casino.”
Article Summary: Manhattan Casino reopened on Saturday, 58 years after it closed. The venue was originally known as the Jordan Dance Hall and served as a major entertainment centre for the city’s African American community. It hosted live dance music on weekends and gospel performances on Sundays. Louis Armstrong and his band performed there three times.

Article Title: In 1959, Sebastian Scirpo started a Connecticut livestock auction in a rented chicken coop and made $7 on his first commission; 67 years later, his daughters run the state's last remaining sale barn
Article Text:
A father's dream

Keeping it all alive

A family operation

Since her father died in 2002, Lisa Scirpo has been working to persuade farmers and dealers that the Middlesex Livestock Auction will continue as the only sale barn in Connecticut. Without it, Scirpo said farmers who want to bring animals to auction would have to travel to Massachusetts or Pennsylvania. But now, farmers in those states come to Middlefield.Scirpo had grown up on the farm watching the animals and the buyers go buy and her father helmed the process. After his death, she went farm to farm with notices, telling people that she could take over. While she initially faced scepticism from farmers, over the past few decades she has proved that she can keep Middlesex Livestock Auction going.Her father, Sebastian Scirpo built much of the place as it is today. The old bleachers, the sale ring where the animals are presented, the chute they go through after the sale and the scale on which they are weighed. “Every cement block you see here, my father built,” she said to CT Insider.Sebastian started the auction in 1959. He began in a rented chicken coop on Little Lane and made $7 on his first commission. He had grown up near his grandmother's farm and loved animals, said his daughter.He also worked in auto body and could fix almost anything. But he wanted a sale barn, so he converted the chicken coop and kept going.In 1970, the family bought the Cherry Hill Road property. Scirpo said her father and relatives built the auction by hand, brick by brick. He did not teach his daughters that livestock were just products moving through a market. “He always taught us that the animals came first because they couldn’t help themselves,” she said. “They needed to be taken care of.”The family has maintained the auction through the ups and downs. When Scirpo was a child, her father lost his feet in a corn chopper. Doctors talked about amputating his legs but another doctor asked if he could try to sew them back together. Sebastian survived and went from moving around in a wheelchair to using a walker, crutches and a cane. He later wore special shoes and learned to walk again. Decades later, Scirpo ran into one of the men who had been there that day. He told her that her father, trapped and in agony, had asked him to shoot him. It was the first time she had heard that part of the story.Sebastian Scirpo lived more than 30 years after the accident, dying at age 66, after becoming ill at the auction. The family later faced another farm accident. Scirpo said her sister, Lana, slipped off a Super M tractor and got her arm caught in the power takeoff. It happened on Feb. 11, their father’s birthday.Lana survived, but lost her arm. She now runs the auction with her sister. Then there was cancer. Lisa Scirpo said she was diagnosed about six years ago. Even while getting radiation, she said, she still came to the auction on Mondays.Scirpo understands that when people hear "livestock auction", they think of slaughterhouses, meat prices and animals being treated like commodities. While she does not pretend that animals sold at the auction are not part of that system, she stands firm with the idea that the people running the barn are careful with them. Years ago, she said, protesters came to the property. She did not throw them off. She brought them water.“I understand,” she said. “But we don’t allow brutality to animals.”When Sebastian died, his wife Kathleen and daughter Lisa took over the work. They built back the business and kept it alive. Until recently, the auction's paperwork was done by hand. Kathleen printed checks by hand, wrote out envelopes and handled money. Lisa's aunt Barbara also helped.But a few years ago, Lisa finally incorporated computers to make it easier for her mother and aunt. The day after they were installed, her mother was supposed to come in and learn how things would work. Instead, her aunt found she had peacefully died in her sleep.In 1970, the auction was one among many in Connecticut, but now, it's the only one left. The state had 5,058 farms in the 2022 Census of Agriculture, down from the previous census, with 372,000 acres of farmland and $704 million in agricultural production. The number of Connecticut farms with cattle and calves fell from 1,158 in 2017 to 876 in 2022, according to U.S. Department of Agriculture data.State Agriculture Commissioner Bryan P. Hurlburt said Connecticut has invested in animal health, biosecurity, food systems that prioritise buying from Connecticut farms and grants for livestock producers, as well as expanded local processing capacity. “These coordinated initiatives reflect our commitment to building a robust, adaptable agricultural landscape that enhances the state’s overall food security,” Hurlburt said.The state Department of Agriculture posts Middlesex Livestock Auction prices online, with categories for calves, cattle, sheep, goats, rabbits, poultry and other animals. Scirpo said that public market matters because it gives farmers another option.The farmers don't have to use the auction and they can sell directly to a dealer. But then, they may be sacrificing the best price. An auction, Scirpo said is a gamble. Prices move, buyers change and markets rise and fall. Here, farmers can see what their animals are worth in public.Today, the auction is still run by the family. Scirpo is 62; her sister Lana is 67. Their aunt Barbara is 83, and all of them still work in the office. On sale days, cattle sales begin at 6 p.m., Lisa Scirpo said. Some Mondays, they do not leave until 1 a.m. Then she still has horses at home to care for. Her father had a saying: "There is plenty of sleep when you’re dead." “That’s the way we were brought up,” she said.The work is part livestock, part paperwork, part crowd control, part market analysis and part endurance test. The auction has licenses for different parts of the business. The animals move through the chute and onto the scale. The auctioneer keeps the sale moving.
Article Summary: Sebastian Scirpo started the Middlesex Livestock Auction in 1959. His wife Kathleen and daughter Lisa took over the work. They built back the business and kept it alive. In 1970, the auction was one of only one in Connecticut, but now it's the only one left.

Article Title: Targets approved, bombs loaded & then Trump blinked: Why US pulled back from Houthi strikes
Article Text:
File photo: US President Donald Trump with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman

Why is Trump hesitating

Poll Vote & Share your view Do you agree with the decision to halt the airstrikes against the Houthis in Yemen? Yes, it was a wise decision. No, action needed to be taken. 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

US President Donald Trump had moved to launch airstrikes against Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen after Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman (MBS) pressed him to intervene. But Trump abruptly halted the operation before the strikes could begin.A report by New York Times states that Trump had spent nearly two weeks wavering over whether to join Saudi Arabia in its renewed fight against the Houthis. On Wednesday, he told advisers he did not favour strikes. But after MBS called him on Thursday and again urged US military help, Trump reversed course and instructed the Pentagon to prepare airstrikes.According to two people briefed on the attack, Pentagon commanders had created approved target lists, troops were loading bombs onto warplanes selected for the missions and US military was prepared for fresh attacks on the Iranian proxy group. the wave of attacks was just about to begin.But by Sunday, however, Trump had reversed his decision yet again. The strikes were put on hold, at least for now, even as preparations for the attack had advanced significantly. The White House declined to discuss Trump's deliberations, while a senior administration official said only that the US had a defence agreement with Saudi Arabia and would defend its allies.The sudden U-turn reflects a larger problem for Trump. The Houthis have avoided attacking US ships and have agreed, for now, not to fight the United States.But they have intensified attacks on Saudi Arabia, leaving Trump under pressure from a key ally that Washington also needs in its wider war against Iran.Saudi Arabia has shown it can use that dependence as leverage. In May, Riyadh effectively blocked a US plan to use American forces to escort commercial oil tankers through the Strait of Hormuz by denying US forces access to its airspace and military bases.The Houthi threat has also expanded beyond Saudi Arabia. The group has attacked Saudi vessels and declared a blockade on Saudi shipping in the Red Sea, while capturing areas near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a crucial maritime chokepoint. The developments have raised fresh concerns over global shipping and energy supplies.A new US bombing campaign would risk opening another front while American forces are already stretched by the war against Iran. Several officials and commanders have also questioned whether airstrikes would force the Houthis to back down.The US spent more than 50 days bombing the group in 2025, striking over 1,000 targets and burning through about $1 billion in weapons and ammunition in the first month. Trump later called a ceasefire, saying the Houthis had promised to stop attacking ships.The Houthis have since rebuilt much of their military capability and are now using artificial intelligence to develop and engineer new missile systems, according to US officials. A renewed US campaign could also prompt the group to resume attacks on American ships and further disrupt shipping through the Bab al-Mandab, adding another pressure point to already unstable energy routes.Trump said Sunday that he remained in “deciding mode” over the larger Iran war. For now, however, the president has stepped back from striking the Houthis, despite having taken the US military to the brink of doing so.
Article Summary: US President Donald Trump had moved to launch airstrikes against Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen after Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman (MBS) pressed him to intervene. But Trump abruptly halted the operation before the strikes could begin. A report by New York Times states that Trump had spent nearly two weeks wavering over whether to join Saudi Arabia in its renewed fight against the Houthis.

Article Title: Pakistan braces for protests as govt warns of $400 million daily loss
Article Text:
Protests in Pakistan (Representative image)

Government warns of economic fallout

Islamabad steps up security

Pakistan’s government has put heavy restrictions on protestors warning them that those seeking to march towards Islamabad with the government warning that disruptions could cost the economy around $400 million a day as separate marches by Jamaat-i-Islami (JI) and Imran Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-i-Insaf (PTI) put pressure on the capital.Pakistan’s information minister Attaullah Tarar said on Sunday that the administration, police and interior ministry were clear that groups intending to cause disruption would not be allowed to reach the capital. He cited a recent Islamabad high court ruling that bars political parties from obstructing public roads and the movement of citizens.The warning comes ahead of a PTI nationwide protest and march towards Islamabad on September 27 seeking the release of party founder Imran Khan, who is incarcerated. JI, meanwhile, has launched a protest campaign against the petroleum levy and has begun a march towards the federal capital.Pakistan’s finance minister Muhammad Aurangzeb separately warned that strikes, sit-ins, long marches and road closures could cause an estimated PKR 120 billion (over $400 million) loss to Pakistan’s economy every day.According to estimates prepared by the planning commission and finance ministry, the services sector, including financial services, communication, retail, transport, wholesale and hospitality, could account for about PKR 86 billion of the daily loss.Industry could lose PKR 25 billion and agriculture PKR 9 billion, while the government could face an additional revenue loss of around PKR 17 billion.Aurangzeb said the disruption would come at a time when businesses were already dealing with higher freight and insurance costs and supply-chain problems linked to tensions in the Middle East, including disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab.He also warned about the impact on IT exports. Pakistan recorded $811 million in IT exports during July and August, he said, adding that previous internet disruptions during episodes of civil disobedience had affected IT exports by as much as 80%.Authorities have begun preparing for the potential marches, with hundreds of containers placed at entry points to Islamabad. Police officials have also reviewed security arrangements at major entry and exit points and other sensitive locations.The Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences and Federal Government Polyclinic Hospital have been placed on high alert, with emergency, trauma, ICU, operating theatre, blood bank and ambulance services instructed to remain fully operational. Pims said the arrangements would remain in place until September 30.The government has also cited concerns over statements by PTI leaders about the planned march. Pakistan’s parliamentary affairs minister Tariq Fazal Chaudhry said a reported remark by a senior PTI leader about turning Islamabad into “Somnath” had raised concerns about possible violence. He said the government had a responsibility to maintain law and order in the capital.The government has said it remains in contact with JI leadership and hopes to resolve the dispute through dialogue. JI has been protesting since August 16 against the petroleum levy and says it wants the government to withdraw the levy.
Article Summary: Jamaat-i-Islami (JI) and Imran Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek- i-Insaf (PTI) put pressure on the capital. JI has launched a protest campaign against the petroleum levy and has begun a march towards the federal capital. Government warns that strikes, sit-ins, long marches and road closures could cause an estimated PKR 120 billion (over $400 million) loss to Pakistan's economy every day.

The United States has issued a fresh advisory against travel to Iran, urging American citizens to avoid the country “for any reason” and calling on those already there to leave immediately amid heightened tensions and the threat of further escalation in West Asia.In a security alert, the US Virtual Embassy in Iran said the regional security situation remained complex and cautioned that travellers could face flight cancellations, airspace closures and other disruptions.“Do not travel to Iran for any reason. US citizens should leave Iran now,” the advisory said.The US Mission urged Americans in the region to remain highly vigilant and closely monitor developments affecting airports, airlines and border crossings.It also warned that procedures at Iran’s land borders could change without notice and advised travellers to check the entry requirements of any country they may seek to enter.The US also cited the activities of Iranian-backed Houthi forces, which have carried out attacks in Saudi Arabia, including strikes targeting civilian airports.“Iranian-supported Houthis have engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including civilian airports.This military conflict has the potential to escalate rapidly,” the alert said.The United States further warned that its diplomatic facilities, including locations outside the Middle East, have been targeted in the past and that Iran or groups supportive of Tehran could target US interests, businesses and institutions overseas.American citizens were advised to enrol in the Department of State’s Smart Traveler Enrollment Program (STEP) to receive security updates and facilitate contact with US diplomatic authorities during emergencies.The alert also urged citizens to avoid demonstrations, large gatherings and areas with a heavy police presence, while maintaining a low profile at locations publicly associated with the United States.In the event of an aerial attack, Americans were instructed to stay away from windows and glass doors, avoid fallen debris and monitor official communications.The alert comes amid an escalating confrontation between the United States and Iran, with Washington maintaining military and maritime pressure on Tehran and Iranian officials warning of retaliation against US interests in the region.The latest warning follows a separate US security alert for Americans and US government personnel in Saudi Arabia.
