Article Title: Ohio flash-flood threat persists as tornado warning ends
Article Text:
Vehicle in Ohio drives through floodwater at intersection. (Photo: Muskingam County Engineer's Office via Anadolu Agency via Reuters)

Storm warning carries 97kmph gusts

Up to 8.9cm rain recorded

A flash-flood warning remained in force across parts of southeastern Ohio into Monday morning after a tornado warning was cancelled late Sunday as severe weather continued across the region.At 11.13pm local time, the National Weather Service (NWS) issued a severe thunderstorm warning for eastern Vinton County and parts of southwestern Athens, northwestern Meigs, northeastern Gallia and northeastern Jackson counties. Radar indicated wind gusts of about 97kmph, while forecasters said a tornado remained possible.One minute later, the NWS cancelled the tornado warning for east-central Vinton and west-central Athens counties after the storm weakened below severe limits and no longer appeared likely to generate a tornado.The earlier tornado alert followed the detection of a severe storm near McArthur in Vinton County. Creola and Zaleski were among the communities that forecasters said could be affected as the storm moved east at about 24kmph.The flash-flood warning covered northeastern Vinton County, southwestern Athens County and northwestern Meigs County and was due to remain in effect until 6.30am Monday.Radar and automated gauges indicated that 6.4cm to 8.9cm of rain had already fallen, with another 2.5cm to 7.6cm possible.McArthur, Albany, Zaleski, Carpenter, Radcliffe and Creola were among the communities covered by the warning.The NWS advised people inside sturdy buildings to use a basement or an interior room on the lowest floor and stay away from windows. People outdoors, in vehicles or mobile homes were advised to seek substantial shelter, while drivers were warned not to enter flooded roads.This version removes the main repetition while keeping the latest-first structure, preserving the chronology and giving each subhead a clear factual purpose.
Article Summary: Severe thunderstorm warning issued for eastern Vinton County and parts of southwestern Athens, northwestern Meigs, northeastern Gallia and northeastern Jackson counties. Radar indicated wind gusts of about 97kmph, while forecasters said a tornado remained possible. Flash-flood warning remained in force until 6.30am Monday.

Article Title: Usher first saw L.A. Reid’s Alpharetta mansion at 13 and dreamed of owning it; at 21 he paid $1.2 million, modernised the 10,823-sq-ft home and sold it for $1.5 million nearly two decades later
Article Text:
In 1999, Usher purchased the Alpharetta mansion for $1.2 million (Image Credit: Realtor.com)

How I’m Living

The mansion that caught Usher’s eye at 13

How I’m Living

The living room underwent a notable transformation (Image Credit: Realtor.com)

Usher paid $1.2 million for the home at 21

He modernised the mansion in his own style

At just 21, Usher turned his childhood ambition into reality, purchasing Reid’s former residence for $1.2 million (Image Credit: Realtor.com)

A home shaped around Usher’s career

Nearly two decades later, Usher sold the mansion

Some childhood dreams stay fantasies; Usher turned one into reality. At 13, Usher had already formed a connection with a mansion he would eventually call his own. In 1991, the future R&B superstar visited music producer L.A. Reid’s home in Alpharetta, Georgia, and was captivated by the property. Years later, Usher recalled on BET’s showthat he walked through the house and thought he wanted to own it one day. Eight years later, at just 21, he turned that childhood ambition into reality, purchasing Reid’s former residence for $1.2 million.When Usher first visited the Alpharetta property in 1991, L.A. Reid, the influential music producer and co-founder of LaFace Records, owned it. Reid had converted one of the rooms into a recording studio for his label, giving the house an especially strong connection to the music industry. Years later, Usher recalled the visit on a 2003 episode of BET’s, describing how mesmerised he was by the house and how he remembered wanting to own it someday.By the time Usher was 21, his career was already gaining momentum. His music was attracting major attention, he had appeared on the television sitcom Moesha and completed his first film, The Faculty. That was also when the opportunity to buy the house he had admired as a teenager finally arrived.In 1999, Usher purchased the Alpharetta mansion for $1.2 million. The 10,823-square-foot residence offered the scale and elaborate interiors associated with a high-end celebrity home of the era.Architectural Digest describes a grand foyer featuring black marble columns, while an open hallway on the second floor overlooked the living room. The living space had a black marble fireplace framed by built-in mahogany bookcases. The primary bedroom also featured a distinctive black-and-gold poster bed. The home’s design was dramatic, with dark finishes and ornate details throughout. Its large size also gave the young musician plenty of room to create spaces suited to both entertaining and his career.For Usher, however, the significance of the purchase went beyond the property itself. He was buying a home he had first seen eight years earlier, when he was still a teenager imagining what his future might look like.The house already had a distinctive appearance when Usher bought it, but he later made a series of changes to give the interiors a more contemporary and personal feel. According to Realtor.com, he replaced the original wrought-iron and glass front door with a wooden one. The wrought-iron and mahogany staircase railing was also replaced with muted grey wood.The living room underwent a notable transformation. The original built-in bookcases were replaced with floating shelves, while the fireplace received a wooden mantel and herringbone-patterned brick, giving the space a more rustic appearance. The kitchen was similarly updated. Its central island was transformed into a muted teal design topped with marble. A farmhouse sink, sliding metal door, bench seating and rustic tables added a more relaxed look to the space. The bathrooms were also redesigned with vintage-style tile, white marble and glass shower doors.Some of the mansion’s most distinctive spaces reflected Usher’s life as a performer. The property included a dedicated dance studio equipped with floor-to-ceiling mirrors and a substantial sound system. That was alongside a home theatre, yoga studio, spa and sauna. Outside, the property offered a heated pool and summer kitchen, adding to its entertainment-focused layout.Usher remained the owner of the Alpharetta property for nearly two decades. During those years, his career expanded dramatically, transforming him from a young performer into one of the most recognised names in R&B and pop music. In 2018, the mansion finally went on the market. Realtor.com and Architectural Digest reported that Usher sold the property for $1.5 million in June of that year.The transaction brought an end to an unusual real-estate story that had begun with a 13-year-old visiting a music producer’s home. Eight years after that first visit, Usher had purchased the same property for $1.2 million. He then spent years updating the 10,823-square-foot mansion to reflect his own tastes and lifestyle before eventually selling it for $1.5 million. What makes the Alpharetta house particularly notable is not simply its size, celebrity ownership or amenities. It was a property Usher had wanted since he was a teenager, making its eventual purchase at 21 a rare example of a childhood real-estate dream becoming reality.
Article Summary: In 1999, Usher purchased the Alpharetta mansion for $1.2 million. The 10,823-square-foot residence offered the scale and elaborate interiors associated with a high-end celebrity home of the era. The home’s design was dramatic, with dark finishes and ornate details throughout. Its large size also gave the young musician plenty of room to create spaces suited to both entertaining and his career.

Article Title: A Toledo woman's neighbour has a tree of heaven covered in spotted lanternflies, leaving her driveway, car and patio covered in bugs and sticky sap
Article Text:
Spotted lanternfly (Lycorma delicatula) is a planthopper native to several Asian countries that has spread throughout states (Image: University of Georgia)

Heather Keyes says the infestation traces back to a neighbouring tree of heaven

The mess spreading onto Keyes' driveway, patio and car

Image: The Boston Globe

How long the lanternfly problem has been building next door

The property owner's response to Keyes' concerns

A Toledo woman says a spotted lanternfly infestation coming from a tree next door has gotten so bad that she can no longer park in her own driveway or use her backyard without dealing with the bugs and the mess they leave behind. Heather Keyes told 13 Action News she has tried almost everything to get rid of them, but the insects keep returning to the tree, a tree of heaven, that sits on the neighbouring property. After struggling to get help, she reached out to the station for support. Here's what she's dealing with, and how the property owner has responded so far.The tree at the centre of the problem isn't Keyes' own; it sits in the yard next door, but the spotted lanternflies living around it, along with the sticky residue they leave behind, don't stay on that side of the property line. "I try to disturb their area, so maybe they'll go somewhere else, but they don't. They go right back to the tree," Keyes told 13 Action News. Her driveway sits just inches from the infested tree, which she said constantly drips sap onto everything nearby, effectively ruining anything she places outside.Keyes said the tree has made basic use of her own property nearly impossible. "I can't park my car back here, I can't even sit back here.It's just so gross with everything. Not just the bugs, but the tree just drips constantly," she told 13 Action News. She said her car, trash cans and patio furniture have all been coated in sap from the tree, adding that whatever she puts outside, she has to accept it will likely get ruined by the ongoing mess.Keyes has lived at her home for seven years, and said the neighbouring tree was the size of a weed when she first moved in. The lanternflies became a noticeable problem about a year ago, and Keyes said she has since killed hundreds of them trying to keep the infestation under control. Her landlord has trimmed back what growth they can reach from her side of the property line, but the core of the problem remains rooted in the neighbouring tree itself, which continues to host the insects.According to county records, the neighbouring property has been owned by Mercer Holdings 1 LLC since February, with a related business, Mercer Maintenance LLC, sharing the same address; both trace back to an address on Upton Avenue. Mercer Maintenance's website advertises tree trimming among its services for rental properties. The maintenance director of the company confirmed he was aware of the property and the tree issue, and said he had spoken with Keyes before, telling the station that Keyes is able to trim the portion of the tree extending onto her own property.
Article Summary: Heather Keyes says the infestation traces back to a neighbouring tree of heaven. She says she has tried almost everything to get rid of them, but the insects keep returning to the tree. Keyes said the tree has made basic use of her own property nearly impossible.

Article Title: Denver's historic bank building was bought for $17.6 million and got a $22.4 million renovation; after WeWork left, the 107,630-sq-ft property is now 100% vacant
Article Text:
The building was originally constructed in 1907 and was later redesigned by architects Fisher & Fisher (Photos: JLL Investor Center)

A historic building

The building also has a two-storey entrance with a 23-foot ceiling

The $22.4 million renovation

Could the bank become homes?

Eight of the building’s nine floors have been renovated and are ready for occupation

Newer buildings sold at steep discounts

Downtown's vacancy challenge

Denver’s historic bank building at 821 17th Street remains completely vacant despite a $22.4 million renovation after its owner bought the property for $17.6 million in 2017. The nine-storey building, now known as The Vault, has 107,630 square feet of office and retail space in the heart of downtown Denver’s former financial district.According to The Denver Gazette, the building was originally constructed in 1907 and was later redesigned by architects Fisher & Fisher. It was designated a Denver Landmark in 1977. The property was one of the financial buildings that once formed the 'Wall Street of the Rockies', when the area around 17th, Champa and Stout streets was a major centre of Denver’s commercial activity.Harbor Associates, based in Seal Beach, California, bought the building in 2017. The owner later invested more than $22.4 million in improvements, including a new lobby, restoration of the first and second floors, exterior facade work and upgrades to the building’s mechanical systems. JLL is now presenting the property for sale as an opportunity for office use, adaptive reuse or conversion into residential or hospitality space.Finding tenants has proved difficult, however. WeWork leased about 40,000 square feet of the building in 2018 but left in 2021 as the pandemic changed office-working patterns.The Vault’s current situation reflects a much wider change in Upper Downtown Denver. Office vacancies across downtown have remained high, although they have dipped slightly to around 38%, according to The Denver Gazette. Some newer office properties have also been sold at heavily reduced prices, with buyers considering residential conversions as one possible way to reuse the space.The area around The Vault once went through another major transformation. Downtown Denver’s historic commercial districts had struggled during the 1960s, when older buildings deteriorated and businesses moved away. By the 1980s and 1990s, however, parts of downtown were becoming active again as Denver developed into a sports and entertainment centre.The former bank building itself became part of that revival. Its large basement vault became the centrepiece of the Broker Restaurant, which opened in 1972 and remained there until it closed permanently in 2017. In 1978, the building also became home to Women’s Bank, which was widely recognised for its focus on women-owned businesses and lending to women.JLL’s property listing describes The Vault as a 'fully repositioned' 107,630-square-foot office and retail landmark. It says eight of the building’s nine floors have been renovated and are ready for occupation, with furnished office suites.The listing says the property is being offered without existing leases. That gives a potential buyer the option to continue with office use or use it for residential or hospitality conversion.The building also has a two-storey entrance with a 23-foot ceiling. JLL describes the atrium as a major feature of the property. The listing also highlights restored historic details, including stained-glass skylights, hand-painted ceiling beams and a sculpted mezzanine frieze.However, The Denver Gazette also reported that a view through the locked doors of the main floor showed areas that appeared to need additional finish work.The possibility of converting The Vault into residential space is being considered as downtown Denver looks for ways to reduce its large amount of unused office space.Bill Mosher, a former chief project officer for the Denver Downtown Development Authority, said historic buildings can have advantages when they are converted.“Generally, historic buildings have real possibilities,” Mosher told The Denver Gazette. “They have lobbies that are interesting spaces.”The Vault has an L-shaped design, with the two wings measuring about 50 feet wide. That layout could provide window access and floor plans that may work for apartments, according to the report. The building is also much smaller in scale than some newer downtown office towers.However, architect-engineer Bradley L. Zieg said converting an office building into homes is not simple because the two types of buildings are designed differently.“Most buildings of any kind of stature were designed and built to a specific use,” Zieg told The Denver Gazette. “Converting offices into residential uses is a real stretch. Residential architecture is fundamentally different than whatever else you would do,” he said.Zieg also pointed to problems involving heating, cooling, ventilation and plumbing. “Even if you can solve the space-planning problem, now you’ve got all the plumbing. You’ve got all the provided heat and cooling. It’s a nightmare.”The challenge for The Vault is that some newer downtown properties have changed hands at much lower prices. Former Los Angeles mayoral candidate Asher Luzzatto has bought four buildings covering a combined 1.75 million square feet.Those purchases included the Denver Energy Center, which was reportedly bought for $5.25 million after having sold for $176 million a decade earlier.Mosher said the low purchase prices make such conversions easier to consider. “The reason Luzzatto is doing those is that he bought them for less than 10 bucks a foot,” Mosher said. “It’s hard to do that with $29 million sunk into building.”Greg Paugh, vice president and broker at Stream Realty Partners, said The Vault reflects the wider uncertainty facing downtown Denver.“For several institutional owners that have been trying to hold strong, they’ve decided it’s time to cut bait and for the few playing the long game, betting on Denver’s recovery, it’s another opportunity to capitalise on another heavily discounted sale,” Paugh said.Paugh said demand may be shifting from LoDo towards areas farther east of Larimer Street. He also said some tenants were moving from Cherry Creek and the Denver Tech Center.“The Vault sits firmly in the CBD, and this may help downtown’s perception if it truly can be revitalised,” Paugh said.He added that he did not expect the historic building to sell at the single-digit prices seen for some newer towers. But he said “it will not be in the first wave of downtown comebacks.”
Article Summary: The nine-storey building, now known as The Vault, has 107,630 square feet of office and retail space in the heart of downtown Denver’s former financial district. It was originally constructed in 1907 and was later redesigned by architects Fisher & Fisher. The property was one of the financial buildings that once formed the 'Wall Street of the Rockies', when the area around 17th, Champa and Stout streets was a major centre of commercial activity. Owner bought the property for $17.6 million in 2017 and invested $22.4 million in improvements.

Article Title: Meet Rajarshi Mandal, the 16-year-old Lexington student whose malaria model showed the same mosquito-net supply could prevent twice as many infections; he won $50,000
Article Text:
For Mandal, the idea began with footage showing fishermen using donated mosquito nets as fishing material because the mesh was available when conventional fishing equipment was not.

At 16, Rajarshi Mandal is already tackling a problem that has challenged public-health systems for decades: how to make limited malaria-prevention resources go further. The Lexington High School student built a mathematical model designed to determine where insecticide-treated mosquito nets could have the greatest impact, and his work earned him a $50,000 Davidson Fellows Scholarship, states an online report by the Davidson Institute. The report adds that Mandal, a rising junior from Lexington, Massachusetts, developed an ordinary differential equation model that simulates malaria transmission under conditions that more closely resemble the real world. His approach considers factors that standard population-based distribution can miss, including insecticide resistance, seasonal changes in transmission and the gradual deterioration of mosquito nets. Scroll down to read the details of his innovation.Rethinking where mosquito nets goInsecticide-treated nets are among the most affordable tools available for preventing malaria, but supplies are limited. According to the report, around 200 million nets are distributed globally each year, with allocations often based largely on population. Mandal wanted to know whether the same number of nets could prevent more infections if they were distributed differently.His simulation examined how malaria transmission changes across different settings and then evaluated where each available net could have the greatest effect. In his model, an optimized allocation prevented twice as many infections as a population-based approach using the same supply.Experts say that finding matters because it suggests that better allocation, rather than simply producing more nets, could potentially increase the impact of an existing public-health investment.From a newspaper image to a research projectFor Mandal, the idea began with footage showing fishermen using donated mosquito nets as fishing material because the mesh was available when conventional fishing equipment was not. The image prompted Mandal to look more closely at how mosquito nets are distributed and what happens when conditions on the ground do not match assumptions made in a distribution plan.His first attempt used a Deep Q Network, a type of machine-learning system. But the model struggled because allocation decisions produced noisy results and the benefits of those decisions could be delayed, making it difficult for the system to settle on reliable value estimates, states the report. Mandal eventually developed a different architecture that directly scored possible allocations, avoiding the instability he encountered with his original approach.Making the malaria model more realisticThe project also presented a problem that had little to do with machine learning. Early versions of Mandal's malaria simulation repeatedly drove infection levels down to zero, which did not reflect conditions in endemic regions.Guidance from researchers led him to investigate backward bifurcation, a phenomenon that can allow disease transmission to persist under circumstances where simpler models might predict elimination, explains the online report.He derived the model's reproduction number and confirmed that the simulation could sustain transmission at realistic mosquito-biting rates. The final framework incorporated seasonality, insecticide resistance, net degradation and the logistical challenges associated with reaching remote areas.Beyond the numbersMandal's interest in the project extends beyond improving a statistic. He points to the everyday consequences of malaria infections, including missed school, lost work and disruptions to farming and family responsibilities. The project also exposed him to the realities of delivering public-health interventions. A photograph of a transport truck overturned in the Democratic Republic of Congo, with mosquito nets scattered around it, underscored how easily logistical problems can interfere with even carefully designed programs, adds the report. For Mandal, the lesson is that mathematical modeling cannot eliminate every obstacle. It can, however, help make better decisions with the resources that reach their intended destinations.Alongside his research, Mandal studies advanced mathematics and computing, plays piano and has performed at Carnegie Hall twice. He also enjoys volleyball, skiing, mountain biking and karate, where he holds a black belt. The Davidson Fellows recognition places his malaria research among a broader community of young researchers, giving the 16-year-old both a scholarship and a larger platform for work aimed at turning better decisions into measurable health benefits.
Article Summary: Rajarshi Mandal built a mathematical model designed to determine where insecticide-treated mosquito nets could have the greatest impact. His work earned him a $50,000 Davidson Fellows Scholarship. His approach considers factors that standard population-based distribution can miss, including insecticide resistance, seasonal changes in transmission and the gradual deterioration of mosquito nets.

Article Title: An 84-year-old Wyoming Navy veteran spent decades building a 207-acre llama ranch with his late wife; after donating it in 2025, the property has now opened as a sanctuary for veterans and first respo
Article Text:
From 'hell hole' to home

A llama sanctuary

Giving away his land for a cause

A space for the community

Al Ellis and his late wife Sondra had spent decades building the biggest vision of their lives, a 207-acre ranch near their two-story log home off US Highway 191 in Boulder, a town of roughly 100 people 12 miles south of Pinedale. Ellis, an 84-year-old Navy veteran and former commercial driver, had turned to become a llama expert later in life.According to him, he has followed what he calls "butterfly moments", seemingly small encounters or decisions that, looking back, changed the direction of his life. On Friday, another such butterfly moment unfolded on his ranch. The land he once called a "hell hole" is now officially Boulder Crest Wyoming, a sanctuary where veterans, first responders and their families will have a place to step away from the weight of service, allowing them to reconnect and learn to grow in the aftermath of trauma.Ellis grew up in San Francisco where his parents ran a bodega and produce stand. “By the time you’re 8, you can take your orange crate down the street,” he said to Cowboy State Daily, remembering how children scavenged for things to put in discarded wooden crates.At 17, Ellis enlisted in the Navy, serving between the Korean and Vietnam wars. His time in the Navy eventually led him towards diving, which became the foundation for much of his adult life.He spent roughly two decades as a commercial fisherman and diver, harvesting abalone and sea urchins along the California coast. He also built businesses with Sondra, including seafood operations and restaurants.He bought a fishery with an old freezer that had, during World War II, stored shark livers for their vitamin A. He converted the fishery into a seafood restaurant named Andrea’s.Then the couple visited a friend in Alpine and fell in love with Wyoming. They eventually bought property near Jackson Hole, where Ellis began exploring the mountains.Soon, Ellis read an article about mountain pack llamas. He quickly acquired six llamas and spent the next decade guiding trips into the Wind River, Gros Ventre, Tetons and other nearby mountain ranges. “It was unbelievable how many people on my trips had never seen a night sky,” he said.As his herd grew, he realised that the 12-acre property wasn't enough. In 1998, the couple bought a run-down cattle ranch near Boulder. At the time, Ellis claims the property was an "eyesore." “I was enticing my wife from a 5,200-square-foot log home on the Snake River to come to a hell hole,” he said.But by 2012, they had transformed the property together, and it was home to about 200 llamas, including 60 pack llamas. The animals became Ellis' business, his passion and, eventually, the reason he and Sondra built the log home where they planned to grow old.The idea of giving away his sprawling llama ranch began taking shape in the summer of 2025. Ellis was watching television when he came across Johnny "Joey" Jones, a military veteran and co-host of Fox News Channel's "The Big Weekend Show." Jones lost both legs to a roadside bomb in Iraq and wrote the New York Times bestseller, “Behind the Badge: Answering the Call to Serve on America’s Homefront.”Inspired, Ellis reached out to Jones by email and sought advice on how to go about gifting his property to serve veterans and his first responders. While he thought nothing would truly come out of the initiative, Jones saw his email and connected Ellis with Ken Falke, a retired Navy bomb disposal specialist and co-founder and chairman of the Boulder Crest Foundation.“As soon as I met (Ellis), it was like ‘wow,’” Falke told Cowboy State Daily. “I was a diver. He was a diver. I was in the Navy. He was in the Navy. There was this really interesting connection.” Within months, Ellis had entrusted Boulder Crest with the property.Sondra died in August 2025 after a lengthy health battle. The timing made the gift even more momentous. “Llamas are the reason this house is here,” Ellis said during Cowboy State Daily’s January visit. “We visualised being old here and wheeling over to the big windows to watch the llamas.” Now the house and land will have a different kind of life.Before Christmas 2025, Ellis donated the ranch along with the two-story log home to the Boulder Crest Foundation. His vision had always been for the land he and his wife built to continue to serve others. “We want other people to enjoy this space, people who deserve it, people who we owe something to,” Ellis told Cowboy State Daily in January.On Friday, Boulder Crest formally introduced its Wyoming campus to community leaders, veterans, first responders and supporters from throughout the region in a grand opening. The celebration included a skydiving performance, the national anthem sung by local EMT and fourth-generation Sublette County rancher Sue Briggs-Stanfield, and a performance by the Wind River Indian Eagle Spirit Dancers. Ellis and his family were recognised throughout the program, as was another guest of honour, the land itself.Boulder Crest Foundation was founded with the idea that trauma does not have to be the end of the story. Its Posttraumatic Growth programs are designed to help veterans, first responders and their families move beyond simply coping with what happened to them and discover new strength, purpose and possibility. The PATHH program – Progressive and Alternative Training for Helping Heroes- helps veterans and first responders transform struggles into strength and thrive in the aftermath of trauma.The Wyoming campus will bring those programs to a region where geography itself can make accessing support difficult. “Al didn’t simply give us a piece of land, he entrusted us with the opportunity to create something that will serve people for generations,” Boulder Crest CEO Josh Goldberg said.Boulder Crest Wyoming will also host family rest and reconnection stays and couples programming. The campus is expected to be fully operational by September 2027. Boulder Crest said the location will serve not only Wyoming but the broader Mountain West as well.Moreover, the foundation will also include Ellis' llamas in its operations. “Watching baby llamas play when they’re in a group is 100% contagious,” Ellis said.The transformation of Ellis' property is already visible. Existing buildings have been renovated, said Boulder Crest Vice President of Communications Jennifer Grady, and much of the operational groundwork is complete.Kris Searles, Boulder Crest Wyoming's executive director, knows something about both the challenges of service and the character of the people who live in this part of the country. “My hope is that Boulder Crest Wyoming becomes a place our veterans, first responders, and families know belongs to them, but also a place this entire community feels connected to and proud of. We’re building something here that is rooted in Wyoming and designed to serve people for generations. ”The regional mission is particularly important in a state where it is difficult to access specialised support. The latest U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs data shows Wyoming had a veteran suicide rate of 45.7 deaths per 100,000 veterans in 2023, higher than the national rate of 35.2.Boulder Crest Wyoming is the foundation's fourth campus, joining locations in Virginia, Arizona and Texas. The organisation says it reached more than 45,000 people through its programs in 2025 alone and has served more than 180,000 service members, veterans, first responders, military families, clinicians and helping professionals since 2014.
Article Summary: Al Ellis, an 84-year-old Navy veteran and former commercial driver, had turned to become a llama expert later in life. The land he once called a "hell hole" is now officially Boulder Crest Wyoming, a sanctuary where veterans, first responders and their families will have a place to step away.

Article Title: Edward Norton ran the 2009 New York Marathon with Maasai warriors to support a Kenya conservation trust protecting 280,000 acres
Article Text:
PC: National Geographic and MWCT

Edward Norton and the Kenya ecolodge that became a conservation trust

From Mount Kilimanjaro to a deeper role in Maasai conservation

PC: The UN

Why the New York Marathon became part of the campaign

The campaign brought celebrities into the race

The 280,000-acre landscape behind Norton’s conservation work

The conservation model still centres on the Maasai community

In 2009, Edward Norton ran the New York City Marathon alongside Maasai warriors to raise awareness and funds for a conservation project in Kenya. His connection with the cause began after he visited Campi ya Kanzi, an ecolodge near Mount Kilimanjaro that linked tourism income with protecting land and supporting the local Maasai community. Norton later became involved with the Maasai Wilderness Conservation Trust, which grew from that initiative and expanded its conservation work across the Chyulu Hills. The marathon brought international attention to its community-based approach. As reported by CBS News, the trust says its conservation efforts cover approximately 280,000 acres of Kenyan wilderness.Italian conservationists Luca Belpietro and Antonella Bonomi established Campi ya Kanzi as an ecolodge near the foothills of Kilimanjaro. Its purpose went beyond tourism. Revenue from visitors was intended to give the surrounding Maasai community an economic reason to keep the landscape intact.Four years after the camp was established, Belpietro and Bonomi created the Maasai Wilderness Conservation Trust to expand that approach. Rather than treating conservation and local livelihoods as separate concerns, the trust developed programmes intended to connect the two.The landscape is part of the Chyulu Hills in southern Kenya, within the wider Amboseli-Tsavo ecosystem. The area contains wildlife habitat, migration routes, forests, grasslands, springs and other natural resources that are important both to wildlife and to communities living there. MWCT says its work is built around generating sustainable economic benefits from conserving these resources.Norton encountered the organisation during a trip to Kenya. The actor climbed Kilimanjaro and stayed at Campi ya Kanzi, giving him a direct look at the way the lodge and the surrounding conservation work were connected.The principle was relatively straightforward: if wildlife and natural resources could generate reliable income for local people, protecting them could become part of the community's economic interests rather than an outside restriction imposed on them.According to National Geographic, Norton became involved with the Maasai Wilderness Conservation Trust and later served as president of its US board. The organisation described its conservation work as a partnership between professional conservationists and Maasai leaders, with programmes spanning wildlife protection, education, health, livelihoods and ecotourism.But Norton saw a limitation in the original funding structure. Tourism was helping finance conservation, yet the scale of the work depended heavily on money generated by visitors to the lodge.Norton had lived in New York for years, so the city's marathon offered a way to take a local sporting event and connect it with a conservation project thousands of miles away. Reportedly, the 2009 race was scheduled for November 1. Norton planned to run alongside Samson Parashina and two other Maasai warriors. Parashina was closely involved with the conservation effort and listed by MWCT as its president and chairman of the board.The contrast was hard to miss. Norton was accustomed to New York's streets, while the Maasai runners came from a community where walking and running were part of everyday life. They trained in Central Park before the race, using some of the same paths where Norton would later compete. The Maasai runners also had to get used to pavement, crowds and the scale of Manhattan.There was even a practical question about footwear. They were accustomed to running in traditional sandals and were considering whether running shoes would make more sense on New York's roads, as reported by New York Daily News.Reportedly, Norton was not running alone on behalf of the trust. Singer Alanis Morissette and illusionist David Blaine were among the other public figures recruited for the fundraising effort, while a larger group of supporters joined the campaign.The fundraising was only one part of the plan. Norton and the trust were also trying to introduce a conservation project in East Africa to people who might never have heard of it.The marathon was not simply being treated as a charity event with a celebrity attached to it. It was a way of explaining a particular conservation model, one in which Maasai communities remained connected to the land and gained an economic stake in keeping its natural resources intact.At the time Norton ran the marathon, the trust and Maasai communities were managing roughly 280,000 acres. The trust says this landscape contains important wildlife corridors, habitat reserves, forests, grasslands and water sources. Its programmes include community ranger operations, wildlife monitoring, predator protection, rangeland restoration and land conservancies.That work is not limited to keeping poachers away from wildlife. The organisation has developed programmes intended to make conservation financially meaningful for local communities.The trust also employs community rangers from the local Maasai population. MWCT says the rangers work under a formal partnership with the Kenya Wildlife Service and use GPS-based monitoring and other technology during patrols.The land is not simply treated as an empty wilderness waiting to be protected. It is a working landscape occupied and managed by communities whose livelihoods are tied to it. Conservation therefore has to account for people as well as animals, forests and water.MWCT's programmes reflect that approach that includes ecotourism, health, education, livelihoods and conservation, with the organisation describing sustainable economic benefits as a way of encouraging local participation in protecting the ecosystem.For Norton, the New York race offered a way to connect two places that appeared to have little in common. A Maasai conservation project in the Kenyan savannah and a marathon through New York's five boroughs became part of the same fundraising effort.
Article Summary: Edward Norton ran the New York City Marathon alongside Maasai warriors to raise awareness and funds for a conservation project in Kenya. His connection with the cause began after he visited Campi ya Kanzi, an ecolodge near Mount Kilimanjaro that linked tourism income with protecting land. Norton later became involved with theMaasai Wilderness Conservation Trust, which grew from that initiative and expanded its conservation work across the Chyulu Hills.

Article Title: Four sisters started a Thai-inspired popcorn brand after a family trip; it now makes $7,000 a month
Article Text:
Image: Courtesy of Party Of. The Lertlumprasert sisters

How a trip to Thailand inspired the Lertlumprasert sisters' popcorn brand

Launching Party Of: branding investment and early recipe development

A production crisis during Compass Group's Retail Incubator Program

Party Of's growth and the sisters' advice for other founders

Poll Vote & Share your view Which aspect of Party Of's story inspires you the most? The family collaboration Overcoming production challenges The unique product offering 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

The Lertlumprasert sisters, Lisa, Lita, Charlene and Charlie, had talked about starting a business together since childhood. That idea finally took shape in February 2023, after a family trip to Thailand left them with a suitcase full of snacks their American friends loved. Combined with their frustration over the "better-for-you" snack options available in the US, the trip inspired their Thai-inspired popcorn brand, Party Of. Here's how the Washington, DC-based sisters built the business from a homemade batch into a side hustle generating steady monthly revenue.According to Lita, a data scientist, the sisters had returned from visiting family in Thailand with an abundance of Thai snacks to share with friends, who loved everything they brought back. As reported by Entrepreneur, what experience, paired with the sisters' shared sense that healthier snack options in the US weren't inspiring, led them to take classic, accessible snack foods and give them their own signature spin. Lisa, who owns and operates Thai restaurants, brought culinary experience to the idea, while Lita's data science background, Charlene's UX design skills and Charlie's product management expertise rounded out the founding team behind what would become Party Of.To get the business off the ground, the sisters began by defining what Charlie, a product manager, called the six dimensions of product-market fit, target customer, problem, value proposition, competitive advantage, growth strategy and business model. Identifying branding as a key competitive advantage, they invested $28,000 to work with branding agency Outline. Recipe development and inventory costs stayed low early on, since Lisa used ingredients already available at her restaurant, bought corn and brown bags, and applied a "ZingPop" sticker, later rebranded Party Of, that Charlene designed on Canva. The StartupCPG Slack group later became an invaluable free resource for learning and connecting with other CPG entrepreneurs.The sisters' biggest challenge came during their participation in Compass Group's Retail Incubator Program, which required them to produce over 30,000 units in under four months, more than they had sold in total during the seven months since launching. To hit that number, the team had to switch to a new pillow-pouch format entirely, which meant reworking the packaging design, getting up to speed on material compositions, and bringing on a different co-packer once their existing setup couldn't handle the equipment or scale required. Things didn't go smoothly from there either, bags weren't cutting cleanly on the production line, shipments got stuck at customs, and tariffs added another unexpected hit. The sisters got through it the way they'd gotten through everything else so far, calling on people in their network and trusting their best judgment even without all the answers.By 2025, Party Of's revenue had grown fourfold from the year before, and the sisters trimmed their cost of goods sold by roughly a quarter, numbers Lisa points to as proof the harder years of building the brand are starting to pay off. Monthly revenue now sits at a fairly steady $7,000, though every so often a bigger order comes through, anywhere from $5,000 to $50,000, on top of that baseline. For Charlene, the payoff isn't just financial; having full say over every decision is a kind of satisfaction she never got from a corporate role. Lisa's advice to anyone starting echoes how they began, nail down product-market fit before anything else, because that early clarity spares you from wasted effort later. Charlene's one regret, if she's honest, is not treating the books seriously sooner.
Article Summary: The Lertlumprasert sisters, Lisa, Lita, Charlene and Charlie, had talked about starting a business together since childhood. A family trip to Thailand left them with a suitcase full of snacks their American friends loved. By 2025, Party Of's revenue had grown fourfold from the year before.

Article Title: US, China launch 'AI dialogue' ahead of Trump-Xi summit amid race to control AI risks
Article Text:
US treasury secretary Scott Bessent announced the agreement after talks with China's He Lifeng in New York. (Reuters photo)

US and China set up AI mechanism

Trade truce and rare earths remain key

Trump and Xi set for Washington summit

The United States and China have agreed to establish a formal dialogue on artificial intelligence, adding a new area of cooperation between the world's two biggest AI powers ahead of a meeting between US President Donald Trump and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping in Washington.US treasury secretary Scott Bessent announced the agreement after talks with Chinese vice-premier He Lifeng in New York on Sunday. The two sides also moved ahead with plans for a trade mechanism first discussed when Trump met Xi in Beijing.The agreement comes as technology leaders warn that rapid advances in AI could create serious risks if research continues without adequate safeguards.US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said Washington and Beijing had formalised a "board of trade" that had been discussed during Trump's May meeting with Xi in Beijing."We just had a very successful engagement with the Chinese on trade and AI, completing where we left off in Beijing," Bessent said at JPMorgan's headquarters in New York, where the two delegations held talks before the summit."[In Beijing] we created the board of trade and began the subject of AI, and this evening those were operationalised," Bessent was quoted as saying by FT.Washington has also proposed a "notification mechanism" to address AI-related incidents involving national security.Bessent said the new dialogue could help the two countries develop "a shared vision of common goals and common threats"."We think that just like any cross-border activity that is moving from opaque to more transparency between the number one and number two AI powers in the world is very important," he added.The talks also focused on whether Washington and Beijing can extend the one-year trade truce agreed by Trump and Xi in Busan, South Korea, last October.The agreement had temporarily eased tensions in their trade war. The US agreed to delay export controls that could have affected thousands of Chinese companies, while China agreed to postpone sweeping restrictions on rare earth exports.China has sought to extend the truce until the end of Trump's second term, according to people familiar with the discussions. The US, however, has been pushing for a shorter extension of about six months.Washington has raised concerns that Beijing has not fully implemented commitments on rare earths. US companies have faced delays in obtaining the materials, which are important for several industries and supply chains. The US has also raised concerns about Chinese restrictions affecting rare earth exports to Japan.AI, Taiwan, Iran and the future of the trade truce are among the issues expected to feature in the Trump-Xi meeting.Trump is due to welcome Xi at Joint Base Andrews on Wednesday before the leaders hold their summit on Thursday, which will include a state dinner for the Chinese president.The meeting comes four months after Xi hosted Trump for a state visit in Beijing. It will also be their first meeting on US soil since Trump's first term, when they met at Mar-a-Lago in 2017.Bessent and Greer have held several rounds of talks with He since the US-China trade war began in early 2025. The New York discussions were their first meeting outside Europe and Asia.
Article Summary: US treasury secretary Scott Bessent announced the agreement after talks with Chinese vice-premier He Lifeng in New York on Sunday. The two sides also moved ahead with plans for a trade mechanism first discussed when Trump met Xi in Beijing. Washington has also proposed a "notification mechanism" to address AI- related incidents involving national security.

Article Title: Washington upgraded 7,474 low-income homes with weatherization, cutting energy costs by $1.4 million and supporting about 180 jobs
Article Text:
Image AI generated

Washington households saved about $189 a year

Weatherisation delivered annual economic benefits

Washington weatherisation projects created 180 jobs

Image AI generated

Washington’s low-income weatherisation programme upgraded 7,474 households between July 2009 and June 2010, with the homes expected to receive about $1.4 million in direct energy savings. According to a report by the Washington Policy Centre, the average weatherised household was estimated to save roughly $189 a year through lower energy costs. The programme also reported wider economic benefits, including around 180 jobs created or retained during the period. However, the 2011 report examined the programme’s costs alongside its claimed benefits, noting that an average project cost $6,070 and that energy savings alone did not exceed programme costs under the scenarios assessed.The Department of Commerce figures put the direct energy savings associated with the 7,474 weatherised homes at $1.4 million. This was presented as one of the main benefits of the programme, alongside the number of households that received improvements.The figures work out to roughly $187 in direct energy savings per weatherised household when the reported $1.4 million is divided across 7,474 homes. However, the report gives a more specific estimate of about $189 a year in direct energy savings for the average household, and that is the figure used in its discussion of household benefits.Commerce estimated that the average weatherised household would receive nearly $385 in total annual economic benefit. Of that amount, less than half was attributed to direct energy savings, which the report puts at roughly $189 per year.The remaining $196 per year was attributed to non-energy benefits, including lower delinquent bills, improved comfort, higher home values and reduced emissions. The report also noted that Commerce acknowledged uncertainty around these indirect benefits because they are difficult to measure. It quoted the Commerce report as saying: “Because non-energy benefits are difficult to measure, there is some uncertainty in our estimates. ”The weatherisation programme was not only intended to reduce household energy costs. During the recession, policymakers also presented weatherisation spending as a way to support employment. The Department of Commerce reported that approximately 180 jobs were created or retained as a direct result of the weatherisation projects during the programme's period.The Washington Policy Centre’s 2011 report, however, examined the programme critically and argued that its economic and energy benefits needed to be considered alongside its costs. It noted that the average weatherisation project cost $6,070 and quoted the Commerce report as stating: “Note that energy benefits alone do not exceed Program costs for any of the scenarios.” The 7,474 weatherised homes and their energy savings are part of a wider debate over the programme’s overall cost-effectiveness, rather than simply an account of household savings.
Article Summary: Washington’s low-income weatherisation programme upgraded 7,474 households between July 2009 and June 2010. The homes were expected to receive about $1.4 million in direct energy savings. The programme also reported wider economic benefits, including around 180 jobs created or retained during the period.

Article Title: ICE officer shoots, wounds man in Austin; protesters demand probe
Article Text:
Federal officers operate after Congressman Greg Casar (D-TX) said that a US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent shot a person earlier in the day in Austin, Texas, US September 20, 2026.

A US Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer shot and wounded a man in Austin, Texas, on Sunday during a brief foot pursuit, local officials said, as the incident drew protests and calls for an independent investigation.The man, identified by immigration attorney Kate Lincoln Goldfinch as 28-year-old Venezuelan Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, was shot once in the torso and remained in serious but stable condition at a hospital, officials said.Austin Police Chief Lisa Davis said the shooting happened after a traffic stop in northern Austin. She cautioned that information about the incident was still preliminary. Austin police were not involved in the shooting, although local investigators were at the scene.Mayor Kirk Watson said he was “very angry and extremely disappointed” that a person had been shot by ICE in Austin, adding that the city had seen a “significant increase, almost overnight” in ICE operations.Watson said he wanted Austin police and other local authorities involved in the investigation rather than leaving it solely to ICE.“I will say, frankly, from my perspective, the credibility of ICE doing some form of investigation just by itself and excluding others would not be appropriate,” Watson said.US Rep Greg Casar, a Democrat representing parts of Austin, had called for an independent investigation shortly after the shooting was reported. He later sent a letter to the Department of Homeland Security seeking an immediate, independent probe, the release of all footage from the shooting and accountability for any wrongdoing by the agent involved.“The horror has come to our city: ICE has shot a person in Austin this morning,” Casar wrote on X, adding that he wanted “truth, transparency and accountability.”The Travis County district attorney's office also asked for local police and prosecutors to participate in the investigation and requested access to evidence held by federal authorities.The Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, did not immediately provide details about the shooting.Goldfinch said she believed Garces Perez had no criminal history or final order of removal, although she later said she did not know his current immigration status.The attorney said Garces Perez's family initially struggled to obtain information from the hospital. His wife was later informed that he had been released into ICE custody several hours after the shooting. It was not immediately clear whether he remained at the hospital or had been transferred elsewhere.About 100 protesters gathered near the shooting site as a large law enforcement presence remained in the area. A dark blue Toyota Corolla with damage to its passenger-side door and what appeared to be bullet holes was later towed away.The Austin incident follows other shootings involving immigration agents. In July, an ICE officer fatally shot 52-year-old Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Houston after federal agents pursued him in unmarked vehicles.Another ICE officer shot 25-year-old Colombian man Johan Sebastián in Maine in July. The administration's immigration crackdown has also faced widespread criticism following the deaths of Alex Pretti and Renee Good in Minnesota.
Article Summary: A US Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer shot and wounded a man in Austin, Texas, on Sunday during a brief foot pursuit, local officials said. The man, identified by immigration attorney Kate Lincoln Goldfinch as 28-year-old Venezuelan Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, was shot once in the torso. Austin police were not involved in the shooting, although local investigators were at the scene.

Article Title: US prepares sweeping sanctions on International Criminal Court
Article Text:
The International Criminal Court building is seen in The Hague, Netherlands (File photo)

The Trump administration is preparing sweeping sanctions against the International Criminal Court that could restrict most of the Hague-based tribunal's financial transactions and potentially cut it off from much of the global banking system, the Wall Street Journal reported on Sunday, citing US officials and documents.The measures would take effect after a six- to seven-month grace period and could prevent the court from conducting transactions in US dollars, according to the report. Transactions involving communications services would be exempt.Meanwhile, a State Department spokesperson pointed to Ssecretary of stateMarco Rubio's view that the ICC threatens US sovereignty.The administration could finalise the measures as early as this week, during the UN General Assembly in New York, or in the days that follow, according to the Journal.The proposed sanctions would go beyond existing US measures, which have targeted individual ICC officials including former chief prosecutor Karim Khan, ICC President Tomoko Akane, judges, deputy prosecutors and the prosecutor who led the case against Israeli officials.Washington's confrontation with the court intensified after the ICC issued arrest warrants in 2024 for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former defence minister Yoav Gallant over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity linked to the Gaza war.Both have rejected the allegations.Rubio said in July that the administration would pursue a broad campaign against the court and would dismantle it "brick by brick" if necessary. He has argued that the ICC overstepped its authority by pursuing officials from countries that are not members of the court, including the United States and Israel.The US and Israel are not members of the ICC.The administration's position has drawn attention to Rubio's earlier stance on the court. As a US senator in 2022, he co-sponsored a resolution supporting an ICC investigation into alleged war crimes in Ukraine committed by Russia, another non-member state. The ICC later issued an arrest warrant for Russian President Vladimir Putin.European countries and other major ICC supporters, including Japan, have pledged to defend the court against US pressure, although it remains unclear what measures they could take to shield its operations from the proposed sanctions.
Article Summary: The measures would take effect after a six- to seven-month grace period. They could prevent the court from conducting transactions in US dollars. Transactions involving communications services would be exempt. Washington's confrontation with the court intensified after the ICC issued arrest warrants in 2024 for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

Article Title: Pakistan airstrikes on Afghanistan: 3 killed, several injured as conflict fears grow
Article Text:
Relations between Kabul and Islamabad have remained strained over militant activity along border. (AP photo/ File)

Taliban warns of 'crushing response'

Kabul denies sheltering TTP

Afghanistan keeps door open for talks
